title: 300,000-year-old tools found in portugal
dek: More than 200 stone artefacts recovered from a riverside location in central portugal.
body: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence of human activity dating back more than 300,000 years at Vale do Forno in central Portugal. The site is located near Alpiarça in the Santarém district, where investigations since 2024 have revealed more than 200 stone artefacts estimated to be between 300,000 and 350,000 years old. Finding artefacts in their original depositional context is particularly important for archaeologists, as it allows the spatial relationships between objects and surrounding deposits to be studied without the disruption caused by later movement or geological processes.

The discoveries also suggest that the Alpiarça region may have been among the earliest areas of present-day Portugal to experience prolonged human occupation. Stone artefacts were first identified in the area during the 1990s, although archaeologists did not initially recognise the extent of the surviving archaeological deposits. More recent investigations have demonstrated that the site contains a substantial assemblage of prehistoric stone tools, with their state of preservation providing researchers with an unusually intact archaeological context.

When I talk about our find, I really mean the original context, which means that the stone tools were found exactly where prehistoric man left them, said Carlos Ferreira, an archaeologist from the University of Lisbon involved in the research. The age of the Vale do Forno assemblage places the occupation within the Middle Pleistocene, a period associated with significant developments in hominin populations and stone-tool technologies across Europe. However, the researchers have not yet identified which hominin population was responsible for the activity at Vale do Forno.

Continued investigation of Vale do Forno could therefore provide important evidence for understanding the chronology and character of early human occupation along the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula. Further analysis will focus on the stone artefacts and associated archaeological deposits, with researchers also hoping to recover genetic material from ancient animal remains. We hope to recover them to understand which species accompanied prehistoric humans in what is now Portugal, Ferreira said.
